entries.fullAnalysis:
The reading this month is augmentation, and it is worth being blunt about what that word is carrying. It does not mean there is visible evidence that AI is making workers more valuable. It means that the thing displacement would have to do — remove people from the labour market and leave them out — has not happened. Prime-age employment is flat, layoffs are low and falling, and more people are being hired than are quitting. That is the absence of damage, not the presence of gain. There is one strand of genuinely positive evidence, and it has a serious problem with it, described below. Confidence is low.

What is new since the last analysis: essentially nothing that concerns workers. Of thirteen panels, exactly two headline numbers moved. The gap between postings for knowledge work and postings for hands-on work widened by three tenths of a point in a single month, on a series that routinely swings several points, so that is noise rather than news. And one AI model's head-to-head rating against other models rose by 2.6 points, which tells you which lab is ahead this month and nothing about anyone's job. Every labour series on the board is unchanged from last month. When nothing moves, the honest output is the same directional reading held at low confidence, and that is what this is.

Take the supporting evidence first. The share of 25-to-54-year-olds with a job stands at 80.4 percent, unchanged over twelve months and slightly above where it was in 2019. This is the measure that matters most for the question at hand, because it is the only one that can tell you whether an outflow from one part of the economy landed somewhere else. Neither of the government surveys involved follows an individual person from a shrinking industry into a growing one, so nobody can say directly that the specific people who left media or consulting are the ones now working in hospitals. What can be said is that in aggregate, nothing went missing. Alongside that, the layoff rate is 1.1 percent of employment and has fallen over the past year, on both a three-month and a twelve-month view. Firms are not pushing people out.

But read the hiring numbers next to the layoff numbers, because together they say something less comfortable. Hiring at 3.4 percent of employment and quitting at 2.0 percent are both low by pre-pandemic standards, while layoffs sit at or below their normal level. That is a frozen labour market, not a shedding one. Companies are not firing incumbents; they are also not taking anybody on. A freeze protects people who already have jobs and does all its damage to people trying to get one — which is the single best version of the displacement case against this reading, and it is not weak. The employment share of 25-to-54-year-olds is dominated by people already working. If employers simply stop replacing leavers, that measure can hold steady for a long time while the door closes on entrants.

Now the industry evidence, which cuts the other way and should not be softened. Employment in the industries most exposed to AI — information, professional and business services, financial activities — is shrinking outright, down 1.19 percent over the past year. Industries AI has barely touched are growing at 1.16 percent. So the widening between them is not a story about a boom in un-exposed work; the exposed side is contracting in absolute terms. That gap is wider than it has been in nearly all of the 2010s, though it has narrowed steadily from its 2023 peak and moved slightly in the healthier direction this month.

The obvious alternative explanation for that contraction is interest rates rather than AI, and I tested it rather than assuming it. Real long-term borrowing costs at 2.4 percent are restrictive, and financial activities — which includes real estate and insurance — sits inside the exposed group and is genuinely rate-sensitive. But construction is the most interest-rate-sensitive industry in the economy and it sits in the un-exposed group, which is growing. A rate story that flattens information-sector employment while construction adds jobs is not a rate story. Rates remain a partial explanation for part of the exposed side, and I cannot size it from what is available. Two other alternatives I considered and set aside: professional and business services carries heavy federal contracting exposure, so a pullback in government contracting would look exactly like AI-driven white-collar job loss, but there is no series on this board showing contracting volumes, and naming a cause without the data to support it is speculation rather than a finding. And the 2023 peak in this same gap sits directly on top of the writers' and actors' strikes, which is a standing warning about how much non-AI noise the information industry code can generate — but there is no current work stoppage.

The one piece of positive evidence for augmentation is pay. In AI-exposed industries, average pay is rising 4.22 percent a year against 3.21 percent in un-exposed industries, and that gap widened slightly this month. Taken at face value, employers bidding harder for exposed workers is the opposite of what replacement looks like. I cannot take it at face value, and this is why confidence is low rather than moderate. Employment in those same exposed industries is falling. When a workforce shrinks because entry-level hiring stopped, the people left behind are more senior on average and the average wage rises without a single person getting a raise. The juniors left the denominator. A frozen hiring market — which is exactly what the hiring and layoff figures above describe — is the precise condition under which that measurement artifact is largest. The available cross-check does not settle it: tracking the same individuals over time, job-stayers are getting 3.6 percent and job-switchers 4.4 percent, a switching premium a little above its 2010s norm, which says people who move are landing well at the median. But that tracker covers the whole economy and cannot be cut to exposed industries, so it cannot confirm an exposed-industry pay story. The composition question is unresolved, and the pay panel is thin support, not proof.

Three further things sit badly with the augmentation reading and belong on the record.

First, two measures inside the absorption picture disagree with the flat headline. The share of unemployed people who have been out of work more than six months is 25.5 percent, up 0.6 points over the year — mildly worse, still normal. More seriously, the gap between the broad underemployment rate and the headline unemployment rate has widened to 3.8 points, up 0.2 over the year and wide by the standards of the 2010s. That is the measure of people landing badly rather than not landing at all — part-time when they want full-time, or drifting out of the count. It is the most displacement-shaped number in the absorption panel. And the prime-age employment share, flat over twelve months, is down 0.3 points over the last three months, which for that series is a sharp move. Twelve-month changes lag by construction; if a turn began in the spring, the twelve-month figure is the last place it would show. I am citing the slower horizon, and the faster one disagrees. My reasons for still citing it are that three-month changes on a monthly household survey are noisy, and that a genuinely different survey — the job-openings data — points the other way, with layoffs falling on both horizons. But that is the doubt that would flip this reading, which is why the thing to watch is exactly that chart.

Second, the productivity test does not corroborate augmentation. Output per hour worked across the whole economy grew 2.2 percent in the latest quarter, down from 2.9 percent, still better than the 2010s average of about 1.3 percent but decelerating and short of the pace a genuine technology boom would produce. If AI were delivering the productivity gains the augmentation story requires, this is where it would appear, and this quarter it went the wrong way. It is an economy-wide figure, so it can never attribute anything to AI-exposed work in either direction, and one soft quarter after several good ones is not a break. But it is a strike against the positive leg of this reading.

Third, and separately unsettling: labour's share of national income is 51.0 percent, has fallen for four straight quarters, and is down almost a full point over the past year against a long-run drift of about a tenth of a point a year. That is roughly seven times the secular pace, it puts the series at its lowest level in records going back to 1947, and it is happening outside a recession with unemployment at 4.1 percent. Recessions have produced faster falls, which is why this cannot be a trigger for anything on its own — but we are not in a recession and it is moving at recessionary speed. This figure is economy-wide, it is heavily revised, it has been drifting down since the 1970s for reasons that predate AI by decades, and nothing links its movement to AI-exposed work specifically. It does not move the reading. It is the number that makes me least comfortable holding it, and it is five months old, so it cannot reflect anything since March.

On the postings picture, which is the freshest thing on the board and the earliest-moving: postings for knowledge work sit about 24 percent below their February 2020 level, while postings for hands-on work sit about 5 percent above theirs. That level is severe, and most of it opened in 2022, before current AI tools were making their way into hiring decisions, alongside the interest-rate tightening cycle — so the level is not evidence about AI and the change is. Over six months the two sides have converged by about three points, which is mild improvement. But I only have where each side stands now, not where each stood six months ago, so I cannot tell whether they converged because knowledge-work postings recovered or because hands-on postings weakened. Those are opposite stories, and that limitation caps how much this panel can carry. It is also worth stating plainly that strong demand for hands-on work is a fact about hands-on work. A knowledge worker who ends up in a hands-on job has not been augmented.

On context: about 21.5 percent of firms now report using AI in some business function, up from 17.3 percent nine months ago, with large employers at 36.8 percent against 20.8 percent at the smallest. Adoption is real and rising steadily, which means the objection that it is simply too early for AI to be affecting employment gets weaker every month. But that survey asks whether a tool is present anywhere in the business, not whether any use of it made a role redundant, and there is nothing linking a particular firm's adoption to that same firm's hiring. It removes an objection; it supplies no mechanism.

The month's most consequential piece of outside news was a payroll print showing total employment down 23,000 on the month, with unemployment at 4.1 percent. That generates a real hypothesis — the whole labour market may be turning, in which case this reading is about to expire. Against it: that is one month, from the employer survey whose two most recent months are preliminary and whose method is known to miss turning points on the way into a downturn, while the household survey's prime-age employment measure runs to the same month and is flat over the year. Those two numbers cannot be netted against each other; they come from different surveys, cover different age ranges, and span different periods. One negative print does not move the reading, but three more would.

The single chart that would move first if this is turning is the prime-age employment share — the share of 25-to-54-year-olds with a job. If that starts falling meaningfully while un-exposed industries are still adding jobs at a healthy clip, then the outflow from AI-exposed work is no longer landing anywhere, and the augmentation reading was wrong.

entries.fullAnalysis:
The reading this month is augmentation, and the honest description of what is behind it is this: the damage that displacement would cause has not shown up in the aggregate labour market yet. That is not the same thing as evidence that AI is making workers more valuable. Almost nothing on this dashboard shows workers being lifted; what it shows is an outflow from AI-exposed industries that so far appears to be landing somewhere. The reading is directional and it is held with low confidence.

What is new since the last analysis: essentially nothing. One figure changed. The survey of how many firms use AI in any business function revised its July reading from 21.5% of firms to 21.8%. Both numbers are dated the same month, so this is a correction to an observation already published rather than a fresh one. Every other panel carries the identical number it carried last time. A month in which nothing moved does not license a new story, so most of what follows is a restatement of a picture that has stayed put.

Start with where something is clearly happening. In the industries most exposed to AI — information, professional and business services, financial activities — employment is not merely growing slowly, it is shrinking, down 1.19% against a year ago. In the comparison industries that AI has barely touched — construction, leisure and hospitality, and similar hands-on work — employment is up 1.16%. Job postings tell the same story cut a different way, by occupation rather than industry: postings for knowledge work sit about 24% below where they were in February 2020, while postings for hands-on work sit about 5% above theirs. Six years on, knowledge-work demand has not repaired.

That divergence is real, but it can only tell you that something is happening specifically to exposed work. It cannot tell you whether those jobs were destroyed or whether the people in them moved. Perfect reallocation — every displaced worker re-employed elsewhere the next week — would produce exactly the same picture on those panels. So the question moves to whether people are landing.

On that, the central measure is the share of 25-54-year-olds who have a job. It is 80.4%, unchanged over twelve months, and still about half a point above where it stood in 2019. Alongside it, layoffs are low and falling. Firms hired at a rate of 3.4% of employment in the latest month against voluntary quits of 2.0%, and that gap has widened slightly over the year because hiring is running ahead of quitting, not because people stopped quitting. Workers who change jobs are still paid a premium for changing: switchers' pay is growing 4.4% against 3.6% for people who stayed put, and that premium has been recovering, not eroding. That last figure is economy-wide, covering all workers rather than only those in AI-exposed industries, so it cannot establish anything about exposed workers specifically. It does say that the general machinery of moving between jobs is still paying people who use it.

I also tested whether this is simply a slowdown wearing an AI mask. A general downturn drags everything down together. It has not: the comparison industries are growing, hands-on postings are above their pre-COVID level, layoffs are declining, and the bond market has an uninverted yield curve with expected inflation near 2.3%. I do not lean on the yield curve to excuse weakness already visible in the data — it prices expectations, not history — but the contemporaneous test on the healthy side of the labour market is the one that matters, and the cyclical story fails it. A rate-driven story that spares construction, the most interest-rate-sensitive industry there is, and hits information instead, is not a rate story.

Other explanations I considered and set aside. A federal contracting drawdown would land squarely in professional and business services and would look like this — but there is no series here that measures federal contracting, so naming it would be pointing at something I cannot see. Immigration policy shifting the size of the working-age population is likewise unmeasurable here, and the employment share is a ratio, so it is largely insulated from population size anyway. The Hollywood strikes explain part of the historical shape of this gap in 2023; they are not available for 2026. And the widely-cited finding that AI chat usage splits roughly 57% augmentation to 43% automation is nearly a year stale, is one vendor's sample of conversations, and conversations are not jobs. I did not count it, and the reading would be the same if it read the other way round.

Now the case against, which is substantial.

The most uncomfortable combination on this dashboard is exposed-industry employment contracting 1.19% while economy-wide layoffs are falling. Put those together and the exposed jobs are mostly disappearing through people leaving and not being replaced, rather than through anyone being dismissed. That is a frozen market rather than a shedding one, and the harm in a frozen market falls on people who never got hired — new graduates, career changers, re-entrants. The prime-age employment ratio measures whether people who already have jobs keep them. It is close to blind to the people who never got in. If displacement is running here, that is the shape it has, and this dashboard is poorly placed to see it.

There is partial corroboration for exactly that. The share of the unemployed who have been out of work more than six months is 25.5%, up 0.6 points over the year — still within normal range, but moving the wrong way. And the gap between the broad underemployment rate and the headline unemployment rate has widened to 3.8 points, up 0.2 over the year. That gap is the measure that widens when people land in part-time or marginal work while the headline job count holds — which is precisely what a displacement episode absorbed into worse work would look like. It is the most deteriorated single readout here. The shorter three-month window on that measure disagrees, which is why I do not weight it more, but I am not going to bury it either.

The employment ratio itself has a shorter-run wobble the headline hides: over the last three months it is down 0.3 points, which is a large move for this series and close to the point at which I would treat it as a turn rather than noise. It is flat over twelve months and down over three. If that shorter window is the truth and the annual figure is lagging, this reading is wrong.

One measurement note that a reader relying on the employment panel deserves. The underlying components of that panel show both employed people and the working-age population lower than a year ago, which reads oddly next to a flat employment share. That is an artefact of the annual January re-basing of population controls in the household survey, which moves both legs by amounts far larger than a normal month and does so on a schedule that has nothing to do with the economy. The ratio is the reliable number and the component levels this year are not quotable. The panel corrects an earlier version of its own note on this point, which is to its credit, but it means the decomposition can only be used as a direction check.

Then there is labour's share of national income, at 51.0%. It has fallen for four straight quarters, is down a full percentage point over the year against a long-run drift of roughly a tenth of a point a year, and is the lowest reading in a series that runs back to 1947. A fall that fast without a recession is what you would expect if capital were substituting for labour. Three things stop it moving the verdict: it covers the whole economy, so it can never be evidence about AI-exposed work whatever it does; it has been drifting down for forty years for reasons that predate AI entirely; and ordinary recessions produced faster falls still, in 2009 and 2010. It is also the oldest evidence in the run, dated March, five months behind the job and posting numbers. So the strongest counter-evidence is also the least attributable and the least current — but it is a record low, and it is falling at a pace this series has only exceeded in downturns.

The productivity panel is supposed to be the test of whether the gains an augmentation story predicts are actually showing up. Economy-wide productivity growth is 2.2%, better than the 2010s average of about 1.3%, but down from 2.9% and now below the range the panel treats as internet-boom-like. It fails to corroborate the augmentation reading rather than supporting it, and it is economy-wide in any case.

Two more things I read and did not count. Pay in AI-exposed industries is growing 4.22% against 3.21% in the comparison industries, which superficially looks like the opposite of displacement. But exposed employment is falling, and when the group is shrinking from the bottom — junior hiring stopping first — the average rises with nobody getting a raise. Genuine pay strength and pure composition predict the same number here, and I cannot separate them, so I report it and do not rely on it. And the AI capability benchmarks — task-length horizons, model-versus-model ratings, model-versus-expert win rates — say nothing about any worker. A model beating an expert on a scored task and an employer deciding to stop paying that expert are different events, and only the second one is labour evidence.

On the news: the latest employment report showed payrolls falling 23,000 on the month with unemployment at 4.1%. It is one month, from a different survey, covering all ages, against a twelve-month prime-age absorption measure — three things differ at once, and netting them is a mistake. It is also fully consistent with the frozen-market picture already drawn from the hiring and layoff data. It does not move the reading, but it is a live warning that absorption may be about to weaken, and a large downward revision to prior months would be a genuine reason to revisit.

One further fragility worth stating plainly: the modest improvement in the exposed-versus-control jobs gap over the last month sits entirely inside the two most recent payroll months, which are preliminary and get revised most, and the statistical model used to estimate new and closing businesses tends to undercount job losses right as a downturn begins. If that improvement revises away, the gap is at the level I would treat as a genuine break.

What would overturn the augmentation reading: the share of 25-54-year-olds with a job falling close to a full point over twelve months while the comparison industries are still adding jobs. The requirement that the healthy industries stay healthy is deliberate — if everything falls together, that is an ordinary recession, not an AI-specific absorption failure. Both the panels involved are monthly and will publish three more observations before the end of the window, so the test will be settled on fresh data rather than stale.

The reading stays augmentation, and it rests on the absence of deterioration rather than on any evidence that AI is making workers more valuable. Nothing moved this fortnight. One panel produced a new number — pay growth for people who switch jobs, still 0.8 points above pay growth for people who stay — and it was unchanged from the month before. Every other series is where it was.

The strongest support is that employers are not pushing people out. Layoffs run at 1.1% of employment per month, lower than a year ago, and that comes from a survey of employers rather than households, so it is a genuinely separate instrument from the employment-rate figures. The share of Americans aged 25 to 54 with a job is 80.4%, unchanged over twelve months and about half a point above 2019. Hiring is soft — firms are hiring 3.4% of their workforce per month, low by past standards — but low hiring alongside low layoffs describes a frozen market, not a shedding one.

That matters because something real is happening in AI-exposed work. Employment in information, professional and business services and finance is 1.19% lower than a year ago — an outright contraction — while construction, hospitality and education and health added 1.16%. Employers are advertising about a quarter fewer knowledge-work roles than just before the pandemic, against hands-on postings running about 5% above theirs. Rates do not explain it: construction is the most interest-rate-sensitive industry there is, and it sits on the growing side.

Two things cut hard against this reading. First, a hiring freeze and a slow displacement running through the front door look identical from outside. If AI is eating entry-level knowledge work, the casualties are graduates who never get hired, who appear in no layoffs rate and vanish inside an employment rate covering everyone from 25 to 54. I cannot separate those from this data. Second, labour's share of national income has fallen to 51.0%, the lowest in the history of the series, down a full point in a year against a long-run drift of about a tenth of a point a year — roughly seven times the normal pace, and happening outside any recession, which is genuinely unusual. It is an economy-wide accounting ratio whose other side is corporate profits, so it is not evidence about AI-exposed work specifically. But it is also the oldest number here, from March, while the employment panels run through July: the strongest evidence against this reading is months staler than the evidence for it.

Nor is there positive evidence of gains. National productivity growth slowed to 2.2% from 2.9%. If AI were making people materially more productive, that is where it would show, and it decelerated instead. And the faster pay growth in AI-heavy industries — 4.22% against 3.21% — cannot be trusted as good news, because when entry-level hiring stops, the average wage rises simply because the juniors left.

What to watch: the prime-age employment rate. It is flat over twelve months but down three-tenths of a point over the last three, and that is the chart that would move first.
entries.fullAnalysis:
Nothing moved this fortnight. Of the thirteen panels on this dashboard, exactly one produced a new number since the last analysis, and that number was the same as the month before: pay growth for people who switched jobs still runs 0.8 percentage points above pay growth for people who stayed put, now measured through July rather than June. Every other series carries the reading it carried two days ago. So the honest description of this run is that the picture did not change, and the reading did not change with it.

The reading is augmentation, and it rests on the absence of deterioration rather than on any positive evidence that AI is making exposed workers more valuable. That distinction matters enough to put at the front. What the data show is that people are not visibly being pushed out of work; what they do not show is anyone being made measurably more productive. Those are different claims and only the first one is supported here.

Start with what is genuinely troubling, because it is real and it has not gone away. Employment in the industries most exposed to AI — information, professional and business services, finance — is 1.19% lower than it was a year ago. That is an outright contraction, not merely slower growth. Over the same twelve months, the comparison industries that AI has barely touched — construction, leisure and hospitality, education and health — added 1.16%. On the job-postings side, cut by occupation rather than industry, employers are advertising about 24% fewer knowledge-work roles than they were just before the pandemic, while postings for hands-on work sit about 5% above their own pre-pandemic level. Six years on, the knowledge-work hiring channel is still substantially narrower than it was.

I tested the obvious non-AI explanations against those numbers rather than assuming them. Interest rates are the most credible: the ten-year yield after inflation sits at 2.4%, real estate and insurance are inside the exposed group, and higher borrowing costs plausibly cool hiring. But construction is the single most rate-sensitive industry in the economy and it sits on the control side, and the control side is growing at 1.16%. If a 2.4% real yield were producing the exposed-side contraction, construction should be visibly suffering, and it is not. Energy and the Middle East conflict fail a different test: an oil shock raises input costs everywhere and does not sort jobs by how much thinking they involve, so it cannot produce weak knowledge-work postings alongside strong hands-on postings. Immigration enforcement would weaken construction and hospitality — the control side — which would narrow the exposed-versus-control gap rather than open it, so it works against the AI story, not for it.

One alternative I cannot dismiss and cannot test: professional and business services carries heavy federal contracting exposure, and cuts to federal contracts would show up as exposed-industry job losses with no AI anywhere in them. There is no series on this dashboard that would let me check that — no federal employment line, no contract-obligations measure, no breakdown within professional services. It is the largest unmeasured alternative in this reading and I am naming it rather than pretending the field is clear.

So something specific to AI-exposed work is going on. The question the exposed-versus-control employment panel cannot answer is whether those jobs were destroyed or whether the people holding them moved. If AI eliminated a hundred jobs in software and every one of those workers was hired in health care, that panel would print exactly the numbers it is printing now, with nobody worse off. Perfect reallocation looks identical to mass destruction on that chart. That is why the absorption data has to settle it.

The absorption data says people are landing. The share of Americans aged 25 to 54 with a job is 80.4%, unchanged over the past twelve months and about half a point above where it stood in 2019. Layoffs are the strongest single piece of evidence for the augmentation reading, and they come from a different survey than the employment rate does — employers rather than households, which matters because it means these are not two versions of the same measurement. Employers are letting go of 1.1% of their workforce per month, and that rate is lower than it was a year ago. Hiring exceeds quitting by 1.4 percentage points, slightly better than a year ago, though hiring at 3.4% of employment is soft by historical standards.

Read together, soft hiring alongside layoffs at or below normal describes a frozen labour market, not a shedding one. Firms are not pushing incumbents out the door; they are declining to bring new people in. That is the shape of everything here — exposed postings deeply depressed, exposed employment shrinking by about a percent a year, layoffs low and falling, prime-age employment flat.

And here is the problem with that shape, which is the main reason this reading is held weakly. A hiring freeze and a slow displacement running entirely through the front door look the same from outside. If AI is eating entry-level knowledge work, the people it hits are new graduates who never get hired in the first place. They do not appear in a layoffs rate, because they were never on a payroll. They are diluted almost to invisibility inside an employment rate that covers everyone from 25 to 54. I cannot separate those two stories with what is on this dashboard, and I am not going to claim otherwise.

There is a second reason for caution on the absorption side. Two readings within it lean the wrong way and sit closer to alarm than anything else in the absorption data. The gap between the broad measure of underemployment and the headline unemployment rate — the people working part-time who want full-time hours, plus those who have given up looking — has widened by 0.2 points over the year to 3.8, which is unusually wide by the standards of the 2010s. And the prime-age employment rate, while flat over twelve months, is down 0.3 points over the last three. That three-month move is noisy and I do not treat it as a reading, but it is the single most likely way this reading turns out wrong inside the next quarter, which is why the condition I set for overturning it sits on exactly that series. Also worth saying: a flat prime-age employment rate is not neutral. Through the 2010s it rose by about four-tenths of a point a year. Flat means the rest of the economy is precisely offsetting the exposed-side contraction, not absorbing it with room to spare.

Two panels that might have supplied positive evidence for augmentation do not.

Pay in AI-heavy industries is growing faster than in the industries AI has barely touched — 4.22% against 3.21% over the past year. That is backwards from what you would expect if AI were replacing these workers, and it is tempting. I do not lean on it, because employment in those same industries is falling. If entry-level hiring in software, consulting and finance has stopped, the remaining workforce skews senior and the average wage rises with nobody getting a raise, simply because the juniors left the denominator. Meanwhile the control group contains leisure and hospitality, low-paid and growing, dragging its average down from the other end. A junior-hiring collapse would produce this exact number. The panel cannot tell the two apart.

The check on that is a tracker that follows the same individuals twelve months apart, so changes in who is employed cannot move it. It says switchers are getting 4.4% and stayers 3.6%, both comfortably above the 2.3% inflation rate the market expects, and the switching premium is slightly better than its pre-2020 norm. On the national median, people who move jobs are landing at real pay gains. But this is an economy-wide measure and cannot be split into AI-exposed and everything else. A healthy national switching premium is entirely compatible with displaced knowledge workers taking pay cuts, and because it is a median it would miss a collapse concentrated in a minority. So the composition question on exposed-industry pay is unresolved, not resolved in favour of the augmentation reading.

The second failure is productivity. If AI were making exposed workers materially more productive at any scale, national productivity is where it should eventually show up. It is running at 2.2%, down from 2.9% the previous quarter. That is still respectable and above the 2010s average, but it decelerated, and I cannot claim augmentation is working on the back of a number that is slowing. It is economy-wide, so it can never attribute anything to AI specifically, and gains being absent is also consistent with the technology simply being too new to register in aggregate statistics. Either way, the positive case is not there.

The hardest piece of evidence against this reading is labour's share of national income. It has fallen to 51.0%, below any level in the history of the series, its fourth consecutive quarterly decline, down a full point over the past year. This series has drifted downward for fifty years, but at roughly a tenth of a point per year — the past year has run about seven times that pace. Declines this fast have happened before, in 2009 and 2010, and those were recessions. There is no recession here: control industries are growing, layoffs are low and falling, the yield curve is not inverted. A labour-share collapse outside a downturn is genuinely unusual and it is the observation I am least able to explain away.

Three things stop it moving the verdict, and readers should weigh them for themselves. It covers the whole economy, so it cannot be evidence about AI-exposed work specifically. It has been falling since the 1970s for reasons that predate AI by decades. And it is an accounting ratio whose other side is corporate profits, which move on margins, taxes and capital income without anyone losing a job. There is a fourth thing, and it cuts the other way: this is the oldest substantive number on the dashboard, from March 2026, when the employment panels run through July and postings through August. The single strongest piece of evidence against the augmentation reading is four to five months staler than the evidence for it, which means it could not yet reflect a turn in either direction. The June quarter print is the one to see.

Two smaller items. AI adoption keeps rising: 21.8% of firms report using it in some business function, up from 17.3% last November, and 41.5% among firms with 250 or more employees against 21.9% among the smallest. That removes the objection that the tools are not out there yet. It supplies no mechanism — the survey never asks whether any use made a role redundant. And the July jobs report showed total payrolls falling by 23,000 with unemployment at 4.1%. A negative payroll print is displacement-shaped, but 23,000 on a base of 158.9 million is about a hundredth of a percent, the two most recent months are preliminary, and this is a whole-economy figure that cannot be netted against the exposed-industry numbers above — different survey, different age range, different time horizon. It is a hypothesis to watch. It is not a reading.

What would change the augmentation reading: the prime-age employment rate falling by six-tenths of a point or more over twelve months, while the control industries are still adding jobs at 0.8% or better. Both parts matter. The first says the labour market has stopped absorbing people. The second rules out a general recession as the explanation, since a downturn would drag construction, hospitality and health care down alongside everything else. Together they describe a labour market that stopped absorbing without a general contraction to blame, which is what this reading being wrong looks like. If both hold on any release in the next three months, the reading should be reversed rather than defended.

entries.fullAnalysis:
The call is augmentation, unchanged from last month, and it needs to be read carefully: this is a finding that displacement has not shown up in the data, not a finding that AI is visibly making exposed workers more productive or better paid. The two are different claims, and the evidence here only supports the first one.

Three groups of workers appear in this analysis and they should not be blurred together. Exposed industries are information, professional and business services, and financial activities — the sectors most exposed to AI tools. Control industries are construction, leisure and hospitality, and education and health — sectors with much less AI exposure, used as a comparison group. A third set of measures is economy-wide and does not distinguish between the two: overall productivity, overall wage growth by job-switching status, the labor share of income, and the pace of AI adoption across all firms. Mixing these up is the single easiest way to over-read this kind of data, so every number below is labeled with which group it describes.

What changed this month: almost nothing. Of the panels tracked, only one moved at all. Job postings for the occupations most exposed to AI — the kind of knowledge work AI tools target most directly — sit about 23% below their pre-2020 level, a gap dominated by a 2022 interest-rate-driven contraction rather than anything AI-specific. That gap narrowed slightly this month, from 28.7 points behind hands-on control occupations to 27.9 points behind. It is a small move inside a spread that has been roughly flat for years, and there is no way to tell from this figure alone which side — exposed postings recovering, or control postings cooling — produced the narrowing. It counts as weak, uncertain support for augmentation, stated as weak. Every other panel is unchanged from last month's reading.

The strongest evidence supporting the augmentation call is the prime-age employment picture. The share of 25-54 year-olds employed sits at 80.4%, unchanged over the past twelve months and still above its pre-pandemic level. This is the measure that decides whether the weakness visible in exposed industries is workers being pushed out and left stranded, or workers moving to different jobs. A separate, independently sourced measure — job openings data showing hiring outpacing quits, and a falling layoff rate — points the same healthy direction. If AI-driven displacement were underway and workers were failing to land elsewhere, this is where it would first appear as a broad break, and it has not appeared.

The strongest evidence against the call, and the one that most needs to be said plainly rather than softened, is that the gap between exposed and control industries has not closed. Exposed-industry employment fell 1.19% over the past year while control-industry employment grew 1.16% — a specific, industry-linked divergence, confirmed by checking that control industries are not weak for unrelated macro reasons (they are not; if the economy overall were sliding, both groups would be weak, and only one is). That divergence has now sat past the level that would normally draw attention for four consecutive monthly readings without narrowing. A gap that persists this long without closing is also exactly what you would see if the reallocation had already happened and simply settled at a new, lower level of exposed employment — workers who left these industries not finding their way back, rather than being in the process of finding new jobs. The data available cannot distinguish "moving, but slowly" from "already displaced, and the level has just stopped falling further." Two more things nudge in the same worrying direction: a broader measure of underemployment — workers stuck in part-time jobs who want full-time work — has been rising and is closing in on its own concern level, and the faster three-month read on the prime-age employment ratio is falling even though the twelve-month figure the whole call rests on is still flat. That is a live disagreement between a fast-moving and a slow-moving version of the same underlying measure, and it is not resolved.

Other panels add texture but do not move the call. Economy-wide productivity growth slowed to 2.2% from 2.9% the prior quarter — still historically decent, but decelerating right as AI adoption rises, which is inconclusive on its own since the technology could simply be too new to show up either way. Pay in AI-exposed industries is growing faster than in control industries, 4.22% against 3.21%, which sounds like a positive augmentation signal, but because exposed employment is shrinking at the same time, a much less flattering explanation fits the same numbers equally well: junior, lower-paid workers leaving the exposed workforce while higher-paid, more senior workers remain, mechanically pulling the average up with no productivity story required. An economy-wide check on whether people who switch jobs are commanding better pay right now — a measure immune to that same composition problem — shows nothing unusual, which removes one piece of evidence that might otherwise have supported a genuine augmentation story. AI adoption among firms is real and growing, from 17.3% to 21.8% of firms over nine months, with much heavier adoption at large firms, but adoption data cannot link any specific firm's AI use to that firm's hiring decisions, so it establishes only that the precondition for displacement exists, not that displacement is happening. A separate measure of the labor share of national income going to workers fell at one of the faster rates seen in decades of data, but slower than in the 2008 and 2010 recessions, and it is over five months old, so it is treated as background rather than current evidence. Frontier AI capability benchmarks continue to improve, but no measure here connects a benchmark score to an employment outcome, so they are read for context only and are not allowed to tip the labor call either way.

This reading would flip if two things happened together: the prime-age employment ratio's twelve-month change would need to drop substantially below flat — a real, sustained deterioration rather than ordinary month-to-month noise — while the exposed-versus-control jobs gap also widens further into genuinely alarming territory. Requiring both together matters: an ordinary broad economic slowdown would tend to weaken control industries too and narrow that second gap, not widen it, so the combination is what would separate real AI-linked displacement from an unrelated downturn. Neither condition is close to firing yet, but the exposed-jobs gap is closer to its concerning level than the employment ratio is, and both series update monthly, so there is a real chance to see this move one way or the other within the next few months.

entries.dissent: The analyst read AUGMENTATION from the panels without being shown either mechanical reading, and the four-corner grid places this month at DISPLACEMENT (gap wide and holding, aggregate deteriorating). Recorded, not resolved: these are different routes through the same data, and neither one overrules the other. The grid in particular turns on a single economy-wide series sitting near zero, so a month's disagreement with it is ordinary rather than a mark against either reading.
entries.analysis:
The augmentation reading holds this month: the data still show industries most exposed to AI reallocating workers rather than shedding them en masse. That conclusion rests on the absence of deterioration in the numbers that would show displacement, not on positive proof that AI is making these workers more productive — worth stating plainly, since it is the whole basis for the call.

What's new since last month is minor and sits outside the panels that decide the call. The postings gap between AI-exposed and less-exposed occupations narrowed slightly, from -27.9 to -27.6, inside normal month-to-month noise. The worker share of national income fell further, now among the fastest declines in decades, but that is an economy-wide figure unrelated specifically to AI-exposed industries, and the update reflects newly available older data rather than a fresh one-month move. A benchmark of AI capability against human experts dipped slightly, which measures what AI can do, not what has happened to any worker's job.

The strongest support for the augmentation reading: the measure that tracks whether people leaving AI-exposed work land somewhere else shows no trouble. Employment among prime-working-age adults is exactly flat over the past year and sits above its pre-pandemic level. Layoffs are not elevated, and companies are still hiring faster than people are quitting. If a real wave of AI-driven displacement were underway, this is where it would show up first, and it isn't.

The strongest thing arguing against it: AI-exposed industries are still losing jobs while other industries keep growing. Employment in exposed industries fell 1.19% over the past year while the comparison group grew 1.16%, and that gap has held at roughly this size for four straight months without closing. It also just crossed a line the analysis treats as historically unusual, even though it improved slightly from the prior month. That is a real tension: a gap that is both newly abnormal and not accelerating is a plateau, not a resolution, and should not be read as reassuring. A broader underemployment measure sits close to the same unusual territory, though its recent trend is easing rather than worsening — ambiguous, not a clean confirmation either way. Separately, exposed-industry pay is growing faster than the comparison group's, 4.2% against 3.2%, which looks like good news for those workers, but exposed-industry employment is shrinking at the same time — when lower-paid workers leave a shrinking group first, the average pay of who remains rises for arithmetic reasons, with nobody actually getting a raise. That gap was not counted as evidence of augmentation.

What to watch: the employment rate for prime-working-age adults is the single number that would move first if this plateau tips into real displacement.
entries.fullAnalysis:
The augmentation reading holds this month. That means the data still support a story of AI-exposed workers being reallocated rather than displaced en masse — but that conclusion rests almost entirely on the absence of deterioration in the numbers that would show displacement, not on positive proof that AI is making exposed workers more valuable. That distinction matters and is worth keeping in view through everything below.

What changed since last month: very little, and nothing in the panels that actually decide the call. Three numbers moved. The postings gap between AI-exposed occupations and a control group of less-exposed occupations narrowed slightly, from -27.9 to -27.6 — a change of 0.3, well inside the normal month-to-month noise of a series that has moved in a range of roughly plus or minus 4 points historically. The worker share of national income fell further, to a level now among the fastest declines of the last several decades, but this is an economy-wide figure that says nothing specific about AI-exposed industries, and the update itself reflects three additional months of data becoming available, not a fresh one-month move. And a benchmark comparing AI model output to human expert ratings dipped slightly (-13.8 on its scale), which is a measure of what AI can do, not a measure of what has happened to any worker's job, so it does not bear on the labor-market call either way. None of these three are the panels the verdict is built on.

The panel that decides the call is the one tracking whether people who leave AI-exposed work are landing somewhere else. The clearest sign of trouble would be a falling employment rate among prime-working-age adults. That rate is exactly flat over the past year, and it sits above its own pre-pandemic level. Two supporting figures back this up: layoffs are not elevated relative to their own history, and companies are still hiring people faster than existing employees are quitting, which rules out the "employers have simply stopped hiring" version of a displacement story. If a wave of AI-driven job loss were underway and unresolved, this is where it would first become visible in the data, and right now it is not visible.

Set against that is a genuine, unresolved tension. Employment in AI-exposed industries fell 1.19% over the past year, while employment in the comparison group of less-exposed industries rose 1.16% over the same period — exposed industries are shrinking, non-exposed industries are growing, and that gap has held at roughly this size for four straight monthly readings without closing. This month the gap also crossed a line the analysis treats as historically unusual for the first time, even though the gap itself improved slightly compared to the prior month (it had been wider, at -2.57, the month before). Both things are true at once: a newly-unusual gap, and a gap that is not accelerating. That combination should not be read as either good news or bad news resolving itself — it is a plateau at an already-abnormal level, and plateaus can tip in either direction. It is not evidence the divergence is closing.

A second soft spot sits alongside this. A broader measure of underemployment — people working part-time who would rather work full-time, measured against the plain unemployment rate — is close to the same historically unusual territory the exposed-jobs gap just crossed. But this measure's own three-month trend has been easing, not worsening, which disagrees with the twelve-month trend pointing the other way. I read this as genuinely ambiguous rather than as confirming the exposed-jobs signal, but it is not a clean reassurance either.

One number looks, on its face, like direct evidence for augmentation and was deliberately not counted as such. Pay in AI-exposed industries grew 4.2% over the past year against 3.2% in the comparison group — exposed workers' pay pulling ahead. But exposed-industry employment is shrinking at the same time, and when a shrinking group loses its lower-paid workers first, the average pay of whoever remains rises automatically, with nobody actually getting a raise. A separate, economy-wide measure of individual pay growth (tracking the same people over time, not an industry average) shows switchers earning about 0.8 points more than people who stay in their jobs — squarely at its own long-run average, with no sign of an unusual acceleration that would need to accompany a genuine exposed-industry pay story. Because of this, the pay gap was treated as most likely a composition effect, not counted as support for augmentation. This is the same reason a raw productivity figure was not used to argue augmentation is accelerating: economy-wide productivity growth actually slowed to 2.2% from 2.9%, below the pace associated with previous technology-driven productivity booms, and because it is an economy-wide number it cannot be attributed to AI-exposed work specifically either way — it was used only to keep the overall confidence modest, not to move the verdict toward displacement.

Two alternative verdicts were considered and set aside. A displacement verdict would require either the exposed-industry jobs gap to be actively widening, or the reabsorption measure to be deteriorating; neither is happening this month. A confounded verdict — some named, non-AI cause fully explaining an otherwise displacement-shaped pattern — was not available because there is no displacement-shaped pattern to explain in the first place: the reabsorption panel that would need to show deterioration for a confounder to be relevant instead shows none. Factors like entertainment-industry strikes and staffing-sector cyclicality that show up inside the "exposed industries" grouping were used to discount how much weight the jobs and wage gaps deserve, rather than as a confounder resolving a finding that isn't there.

Background context worth naming without over-weighting: AI adoption among firms continues to climb steadily (roughly 17% to 22% of firms since late 2025), concentrated more heavily at large firms, which establishes that the underlying technology is being deployed at meaningfully greater scale — a plausibility check, not itself a labor-market finding. The bond market shows no inversion and stable inflation expectations, arguing against a general economic slump explaining the exposed-industry softness, though this cannot rule out a slowdown specific to a few subsectors within the "exposed" grouping. A wire report on AI's impact on hiring exists in this month's news but was not tested against any specific figure in this analysis and did not move the reading either direction.
